newsitem.title: USA: Freezing weather hampers Midwest flooding battle.
newsitem.headline: Freezing weather hampers Midwest flooding battle.

text.p: Thousands of volunteers in the northern plains states were furiously filling sandbags on Saturday, as frigid weather and more snow and rain hampered the battle to hold back extensive flooding.
Rapidly melting snow combined with steadily falling rain forced some evacuations from the Minnesota town of Montevideo where residents were sandbagging levees.

Cold weather in North Dakota was expected to make more difficult the efforts to build dikes and sandbag barriers that could fortify homes and farms in the path of flooded rivers and melting snowpacks.

"If it gets frozen, it's very hard to place sandbags properly," said Dennis Walaker, manager of operations for the city of Fargo, N.D. "If we can have the rest of the day to continue our work, it will help." But he added that the city really needed another day after that.
But the falling temperatures could actually help slow the spring thaw in the fertile Red River Valley that divides North Dakota and Minnesota.

"That's our hope," said North Dakota State University geologist Donald Schwert in Fargo. "Basically, in our view, we're not really happy about all this water coming down right now. The positive aspect about this is temperatures are expected to pass freezing or a little bit below for the next few days and that should slow the melt off."
Dozens of towns and acres of farmland were surrounded or covered by icy waters and bracing for more snow and rain.
In West Fargo, tractors with water pumps attached were being used to pump water from the Sheyenne River to an area built to divert flood waters.
In the eastern part of North Dakota, which includes Fargo, just less than an inch of rain and freezing rain has fallen since Friday.
But further west, blizzard conditions closed down part of U.S. Interstate 94 with as much as 10 inches of snow accumulating, and that moisture is moving east.
"We're still expecting a good amount of precipitation throughout the central part of the state and the east," said Todd Hamilton, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Bismarck, N.D.
In the north central part of the state, the extra rain and snow was slowing the fall of water levels in rivers that had already crested.
"The moisture expected will just affect the fall rate," said Charlene Prindivalle, a hydrologist with the National Weather Service in Bismarck.

But the Red River, already several feet above flood stage, is not expected to crest until the end of next week, leaving people in the Red River Valley the prospect on Saturday of fighting both a blizzard and a flood.
"The river's still going up over 3 feet every 24 hours, which is going up faster than anyone has seen in a 24-hour period," Walaker said.
Flooding in the area drags out longer than in other parts of the country because the Red River flows north.
"Because of the odd nature of that Red River flowing north, you have melt occur in the south and it's pushing against ice up north," Pat Scott of North Dakota's Division of Emergency Management said.
No deaths or serious injuries had been reported since a woman and her teen-age daughter died after plunging off a washed-out road with their horse trailer Monday night.
